provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that before a State may irrevocably terminate parental rights, due process under the Fourteenth Amendment requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence; a fair preponderance standard is unconstitutional.
key_cases.relevance: This is the federal constitutional source of the clear-and-convincing standard Nebraska applies in every termination case.
key_cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that there is no absolute federal due process right to appointed counsel in parental rights termination proceedings; the Eldridge factors are weighed case by case against a presumption that appointed counsel is required only where physical liberty is at stake, and on these facts no counsel was required.
key_cases.relevance: It is the federal baseline on counsel in termination cases, which Nebraska exceeds by statute under Neb. Rev. Stat. § 43-279.01.
key_cases.quote: the presumption that there is a right to appointed counsel only where the indigent, if he is unsuccessful, may lose his personal freedom

key_cases.case_name: In re Interest of Jessalina M.
key_cases.holding: The court held that the § 43-292(7) statutory ground was properly found, that changed conditions between petition and hearing bear on fitness and best interests rather than on the statutory ground, and affirmed the termination of parental rights.
key_cases.relevance: It fixes the timing rule for the § 43-292(7) ground and confirms that unfitness and best interests are reviewed separately from the mechanical statutory basis.
key_cases.quote: if conditions have changed since the time the petition was filed to the time of the hearing, the court is advised to factor those changes into its determination of fitness

key_cases.case_name: In re Interest of Leyton C. & Landyn C.
key_cases.holding: The court held that the State proved by clear and convincing evidence both a statutory ground under § 43-292 and that termination was in the children's best interests, and reversed the Court of Appeals' contrary decision.
key_cases.relevance: It states and applies the two-part clear-and-convincing test — statutory ground plus best interests — that governs every Nebraska termination.
key_cases.quote: The State proved by clear and convincing evidence that Madison neglected to provide necessary parental care and protection for her children.

key_cases.case_name: In re Adoption of Kate S.
key_cases.holding: The court held that petitioners seeking to dispense with a parent's adoption consent on abandonment grounds must prove willful abandonment by clear and convincing evidence, and affirmed the county court's finding that the father had not abandoned the child.
key_cases.relevance: It states Nebraska's standard for proceeding to adoption without a parent's consent, the stepparent-adoption analogue to termination.
key_cases.quote: The conduct constituting abandonment must appear by clear and convincing evidence to be willful, intentional, or voluntary, without just cause or excuse.

key_cases.case_name: In re Adoption of Micah H.
key_cases.holding: The court held that the Nebraska Indian Child Welfare Act's active-efforts provisions in § 43-1503(1) are not a checklist requiring compliance with every subsection but a case-by-case standard, affirmed the findings of active efforts and of willful abandonment proved by clear and convincing evidence, but vacated the adoption decree because the county court did not strictly comply with the consent and criminal-history requirements of Neb. Rev. Stat. § 43-107.
key_cases.relevance: It is the source of the willful-abandonment standard that In re Adoption of Kate S. applies when petitioners seek to dispense with a parent's consent to adoption.
key_cases.quote: The conduct constituting abandonment as defined above must appear by clear and convincing evidence to be willful, intentional, or voluntary, without just cause or excuse.

key_cases.case_name: In re Interest of Jahon S.
key_cases.holding: The court held that the § 43-292(2) statutory ground was established by the father's neglect of the child's siblings and that termination of the incarcerated father's parental rights was in the child's best interests, affirming the termination.
key_cases.relevance: This is the published Nebraska Supreme Court holding, in the majority opinion, that incarceration alone cannot be the sole basis for terminating parental rights but is a factor, together with the rule that the criminal conduct causing the incarceration is voluntary.
key_cases.quote: Although incarceration alone cannot be the sole basis for terminating parental rights, it is a factor to be considered.
